muhammad.name: Muhammad ﷺ
muhammad.bio: Son of Abdullah and Aminah, of the Banu Hashim clan of Quraysh. This application traces his life from his birth to his death.

bioSections.heading: Place in the Sīrah
bioSections.body: The timeline episodes directly connected with this person are: Birth of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ — Muhammad ﷺ was born in Makkah among the Banu Hashim of Quraysh. The biographical tradition places his birth in the Year of the Elephant, around 570–571 CE; Monday is reported in Sahih Muslim, while the exact month and day remain disputed. According to the most widespread biographical account, his father ʿAbd Allah had already died, and his mother Aminah cared for him in his earliest days. Death of Abdullah, the Prophet's ﷺ father — ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAbd al-Muttalib died while Aminah was pregnant or shortly after the birth, according to differing biographical reports. The most widespread account places his death in Yathrib, where he had stayed ill after a journey. Seerah accounts describe him travelling north with a trading caravan. This entry preserves the chronological disagreement rather than imposing one exact date or scenario. Nursing among the Banu Sa'd — In the biographical tradition, Muhammad ﷺ was entrusted to Halimah al-Saʿdiyyah, a wet nurse from Banu Saʿd ibn Bakr. He spent part of his early childhood in a Bedouin setting around Makkah. Seerah biographies describe a practice in which Meccan families entrusted young children to wet nurses living in the desert. These references help trace this person’s role across the Sīrah while preserving the qualifications attached to each report.

khadijah.name: Khadijah bint Khuwaylid
khadijah.role: First wife of the Prophet ﷺ
khadijah.bio: A respected businesswoman of Makkah. She married Muhammad ﷺ before the revelation and supported him from the first moments of the mission. She died shortly before the Hijrah.

bioSections.heading: Place in the Sīrah
bioSections.body: The timeline episodes directly connected with this person are: Marriage to Khadijah — Biographies place Muhammad’s ﷺ marriage to Khadijah bint Khuwaylid after the trading journey to al-Sham. They emphasise the trust placed in his work and Khadijah’s role as his first wife and major supporter. Some family and chronological details vary across reports. Biographical accounts describe Khadijah as a merchant who entrusted her goods to agents. Retreats in the Cave of Hira — Before the revelation, the Prophet ﷺ regularly withdraws for several nights to the Cave of Hira, on Jabal al-Nur. This account is reported in the hadith of Aisha on the beginning of the revelation (Sahih al-Bukhari). These retreats immediately precede the first revelation. It should be read within the family, social and geographical setting described by the accounts from this period. The first revelation — In the Cave of Hira, the angel Jibril brings the Prophet ﷺ the first verses of Surah Al-'Alaq. Most scholars place the beginning of the revelation in the month of Ramadan; the exact day is disputed. It is the starting point of the prophetic mission. These references help trace this person’s role across the Sīrah while preserving the qualifications attached to each report.

abu_bakr.name: Abu Bakr as-Siddiq
abu_bakr.bio: A longtime Companion of the Prophet ﷺ. He accompanied him on the Hijrah, notably in the Cave of Thawr, and became the first caliph after his death.

bioSections.heading: Place in the Sīrah
bioSections.body: The timeline episodes directly connected with this person are: The first believers — Khadijah, Ali, Zayd ibn Harithah and Abu Bakr are among the first to believe in his message. Abu Bakr then invites close acquaintances to Islam, among them well-known Companions, according to Ibn Ishaq. These first believers form the core of the nascent community. This episode belongs to the period “The first revelation”. The discreet call — During a first phase, the Prophet ﷺ discreetly calls his relatives and friends to Islam. According to Ibn Ishaq, this phase lasted about three years. It allowed a first core of believers to form. This episode belongs to the period “Beginning of the preaching”. It should be read within the family, social and geographical setting described by the accounts from this period. Persecution of the vulnerable believers — Believers without tribal protection, such as Bilal, Sumayyah and her family, suffer ill-treatment. Abu Bakr frees several persecuted people, including Bilal ibn Rabah, according to tradition. These trials explain the first migrations. This episode belongs to the period “Persecution and trials”. It should be read within the family, social and geographical setting described by the accounts from this period. abu_talib.name: Abu Talib
abu_talib.bio: The Prophet's ﷺ paternal uncle, who took him in after the death of Abd al-Muttalib and then protected him against Quraysh. According to the reported accounts, he died without having embraced Islam.

bioSections.heading: Place in the Sīrah
bioSections.body: The timeline episodes directly connected with this person are: Guardianship of Abd al-Muttalib, then Abu Talib — Biographical accounts say that Abd al-Muttalib entrusted his grandson to Abu Talib before his own death. They place the grandfather’s death when Muhammad ﷺ was about eight; the exact age and its conversion to a Common Era year remain traditional chronological markers, not an absolute date. Journey to Syria with Abu Talib — Sirah biographies report a trading journey to al-Sham with his uncle Abu Talib when Muhammad ﷺ was young. The story of meeting the monk Bahira is well known, but its details and authenticity are debated; it should not be presented as a fact established by an unanimously authenticated hadith. The protection of Abu Talib — Facing pressure from Quraysh, Abu Talib continues to protect his nephew. He refuses to hand him over, although according to the reported accounts he did not embrace Islam. This tribal protection was essential in Makkah. This episode belongs to the period “Beginning of the preaching”. These references help trace this person’s role across the Sīrah while preserving the qualifications attached to each report.

ali.bio: The Prophet's ﷺ cousin, raised in his household. He is counted among the very first believers and slept in the Prophet's ﷺ bed on the night of Quraysh's plot.

bioSections.heading: Place in the Sīrah

This episode belongs to the period “Persecution and trials”. It should be read within the family, social and geographical setting described by the accounts from this period. Migration of the Companions to Yathrib — After the second pledge, the Muslims leave Makkah in small groups for Yathrib. The departure is discreet to avoid opposition from Quraysh. The community re-forms in Yathrib. This episode belongs to the period “The Hijrah”. It should be read within the family, social and geographical setting described by the accounts from this period. The Banu Qaynuqa episode — A conflict with Banu Qaynuqa is placed after Badr, in the context of agreements in Madinah. Reports describe a breakdown of the Medinan pact and a siege, followed by the tribe’s departure from the oasis. Details and motives vary across the later narrative sources. zaynab_bint_khuzayma.name: Zaynab bint Khuzayma
zaynab_bint_khuzayma.role: Wife of the Prophet ﷺ, known as the Mother of the Poor
zaynab_bint_khuzayma.bio: Zaynab bint Khuzayma al-Hilaliyya was one of the wives of the Prophet ﷺ. Known as Umm al-Masakin (“Mother of the Poor”), biographical notices remember her for generosity toward people in need. Her marriage to the Prophet was brief; sources differ about its exact duration and some chronological details.

bioSections.heading: Place in the Sīrah
bioSections.body: Biographical notices place her among the women who married the Prophet ﷺ in Madinah. They report an earlier marriage to ʿUbayda ibn al-Harith, who died at Badr, followed by her marriage to the Prophet. Sources do not agree on the exact year of the marriage or the length of their life together: some reports say a few months, while others give a longer period. She died during the Prophet’s lifetime.

bioSections.heading: Family connections
bioSections.body: She is known as a wife of the Prophet ﷺ. One biographical notice also describes her as a maternal sister of Maymuna bint al-Harith. The application presents this as a reported maternal relationship, not as a paternal lineage.

bioSections.heading: Reading notes
bioSections.body: Her title Umm al-Masakin is associated with generosity toward the poor. Reports differ about the marriage and death dates and the exact duration of the marriage. The application preserves these differences rather than imposing false chronological precision.

umayma_bint_abd_al_muttalib.name: Umayma bint Abd al-Muttalib
umayma_bint_abd_al_muttalib.role: Paternal aunt of the Prophet ﷺ, mother of Zaynab bint Jahsh
umayma_bint_abd_al_muttalib.bio: Umayma bint Abd al-Muttalib was a paternal aunt of the Prophet ﷺ, a daughter of Abd al-Muttalib and a sister of Abdullah and Abu Talib. Genealogical notices identify her as the mother of Zaynab bint Jahsh, who married the Prophet ﷺ; Zaynab was therefore his cousin. Information about Umayma’s life is sparse, and her possible conversion to Islam is disputed.

bioSections.heading: Family position
bioSections.body: Umayma belonged to the Hashimite family: she was a daughter of Abd al-Muttalib and a sister of Abdullah, the Prophet’s father, as well as Abu Talib. She was therefore Muhammad’s paternal aunt. Genealogical notices identify her as the wife of Jahsh ibn Riʿab and the mother of Zaynab bint Jahsh.

bioSections.heading: Connection to the Sīrah
bioSections.body: Her place in the Sīrah is primarily genealogical. Her daughter Zaynab bint Jahsh married the Prophet ﷺ after her marriage to Zayd ibn Haritha. This family connection explains the cousin relationship between Zaynab and Muhammad ﷺ. The profile therefore links Umayma to her daughter’s biography and to the family tree without assigning her a narrative role that the sources do not describe.

bioSections.heading: Reading notes
bioSections.body: The early biographical notices about Umayma are few. Ibn Saʿd includes her among women of the Prophet’s family, while Ibn Ishaq does not count her among the aunts who accepted Islam, according to the summary transmitted by Ibn Hajar. Her conversion is therefore disputed. Details of her life should not be supplied by conjecture.

abu_sufyan.name: Abu Sufyan ibn Harb
abu_sufyan.role: Quraysh notable and father of Umm Habiba
abu_sufyan.bio: Abu Sufyan ibn Harb (Sakhr ibn Harb) was a prominent Quraysh leader in Makkah. He led the caravan associated with the events preceding Badr, commanded the Meccan forces at Uhud and took part in the confederate coalition at the Trench. Biographical reports place his conversion to Islam on the eve of the conquest of Makkah. He was the father of Umm Habiba, a wife of the Prophet ﷺ.

bioSections.heading: Place in the Sīrah
bioSections.body: The sources present Abu Sufyan as a merchant and a leading figure of Quraysh. The caravan he led forms part of the context of Badr; he later commanded the Meccan forces at Uhud and played a role in the confederate coalition at the Trench. Reports say he entered Islam on the eve of the conquest of Makkah and later took part in the events of Hunayn.

bioSections.heading: Family connections and alliances
bioSections.body: He was the father of Ramla, known as Umm Habiba, one of the wives of the Prophet ﷺ. He was therefore the Prophet’s father-in-law by marriage. This family connection is shown separately from his political and military relations with the Muslim community.

bioSections.heading: Reading notes
bioSections.body: Sources differ on some details of his negotiations, conversion and role in events before the conquest. Sīrah accounts and later traditions do not always provide the same level of precision. This profile distinguishes events supported by hadith from details drawn from historical chronicles.
